paired_caption: 21. Cubicle (q), painting of wall E in a drawing by G. Mariani. In a mountainous landscape, three hunters with skewers and dogs approach a simulacrum of Artemis-Isis, erected in a grove, near a betilo surmounted by a radiated crown. One of them, in which Hippolytus was recognized, offers a crown to the statue of the goddess; a little further back is another female statue (Aphrodite, to whom the young man refuses homage) standing near another betilo surmounted by an element that is not clearly distinguishable (a cyst?); on the right there is a large tripod, a reference to Apollo, placed on a round base. In the background, between cliffs and bushes, another betilo, while halfway up the composition a deer jumps that seems to come out of a cave. Although the landscape element is decidedly predominant and can make the painting interpreted as a simple sacred landscape, the decorative program of the cubicle made explicit in the comparison of the two pairs of paintings (Daedalus and Icarus / Marsyas, Hippolytus / Heracles and the Hesperides), leans towards the mythological subject, of which this is the only representation known so far, rather than for a generic landscape representation.

paired_caption: 179a-d. During the excavation of the garden in front of the triclinium (31), carried out in 1985, numerous and minute fragments of painted plaster were recovered in the filling soil, pertaining to an articulated and refined wall of phase IIB of the III style. The elements available allow the reconstruction of a large room, with decoration with a symmetrical structure, probably divided into an antechamber and hall; one can therefore think of a triclinium redecorated following heavy damage, or rebuilt following substantial structural changes. A panel with a black background was almost entirely recomposed flanked by an architectural foreshortening with a blue background beyond which another panel with a black background returned. The fragmentary nature of the plaster does not prevent us from appreciating the richness of the decorative motifs, animated and otherwise, and the high technical quality of the very accurate drawing even in details far removed from the viewer's eye, such as those of the frames and squares in the upper area. The black plinth with taut garlands and small squares is distinguished from the predella by a band with upside-down lotus buds and semicircles. The predella follows the course of the architecture of the middle area, curving in correspondence with the pinkish marble base with reliefs of sphinxes facing corresponding to the colonnaded hemicycle of the foreshortening. Groups of Maenads, Silenus and Satyr (fig. 179d), in different attitudes and activities, each of which is concluded in itself, constitute a unitary subject, which can also be read below. A stretched Maenad playing the lyra facing a Silenus playing the double flute seem to accompany the coronation of the seated Maenad, performed by another standing; extremely lively is the dance of the following Maenad who, seen from behind with her mantle raised, holds a tray in her left hand, towards which she looks; followed by the group consisting of the Maenad cloaked in green looking towards the Satyr running with a Maenad on his back; of a fourth figure only a hand remains, while on the far right there is still a seated Maenad, dressed in green, looking downwards. The black panel of the middle area (fig. 1'79a) is framed by taut garlands, rising from a crater flanked by panthers, consisting of daisies and bunches of grapes to which pomegranates are added after the interruption, at a third of the height, marked by the presence of a pair of winged griffins standing on a goblet base; higher up another interruption is given by a Mermaid in frontal view, while the terminal element is represented by an eagle placed in front of the capital of the column that guarantees the first element of the side foreshortening. In the latter (fig. 1'79b) Ionic columns, beyond which windowed walls can be seen, stand out to support a curved architrave, decorated with masks alternating with panthers, on which rest two theatrical masks and a female figure with cornucopia and modio on her head, placed in correspondence with the column with collars and lotus buds, which closes the foreshortening on the left and which at the base presents the mask of a young Satyr. Particular for its exuberant decorative richness is the red partition (fig. 179c) that closes it at the bottom; on its surface there are vine branches, pine branches with a pine cone, wild roses, ivy with corymbs, pears, oleanders, on which stand out the masks of a young Satyr and an elderly Silenus, a silver situla, a five-reed syringe, a cist and a goat's head. The dividing element towards the next black panel consists of a reed around which an oak branch with acorns and one of white bellflower in bloom are wrapped on which a snail and a lizard move. The upper area has a yellow background with garlands and shoots that delimit an ovular element with a black background with a Maenad prone towards a kneeling Satyr, in correspondence with the black panel, while in correspondence with the foreshortening, on a red background, there is a painting with the busts of a Satyr crowned with pine and a Maenad crowned with ivy. Also in this area the shoots are enriched with fruits, accompanied by floral cusps and paintings with animals.

paired_caption: 49. Exedra (e), wall E, central section, middle area, detail: painting depicting Heracles (deceased) and Nessus. The centaur on his knees, his back covered by the pardalis knotted around his neck, offers himself to Heracles as the ferryman of Deianira, wife of Heracles and daughter of Dionysus. The gesture of the centaur indicates the depth of the waters. With her on his back, Nessus crosses the river and, having arrived on the other bank, tries to use violence against her; but it is struck in the chest by Heracles' arrow, shot from half a mile away. So he advises Deianira to wet Heracles' shirt in the well of blood and sperm poured on the ground, to ensure her husband's fidelity. But it is a poison that will cause the death and apotheosis of Heracles, assisted by his son Hyllus. In the painting appears the head of Deianira, who holds the little Hyllus to his chest in the chariot pulled by two horses. Behind the horses you can see a tree, a mountain (on the right) and a building (on the left). The other four older known replicas of the scene appear only in paintings of the III style of good quality: VI 9,3, (26): VIII 5,16, (b); IX 2:16, (e); IX 5:18, (g). The model was probably a painting by Artemon, a painter active in Asia Minor in the first half of the third century B.C. (Plin., Nat. hist., XXXV, 139). Veils, Maenads, pinakes and tripods depicted in the area above the painting, are initiatory tools; being hybrid, participating in human and animal nature, the Centaur is a mediator or bridge between two worlds. The wide gesture of the arms is surprising, identical to that of the Silenus Marsyas, another mediator between two levels, depicted in the alcove of the cubicle (f).  26 AFS C1527

paired_caption: 27. Room (d), view from the E before the reconstruction of the partition S. In the small room, it was preferred not to emphasize the center of the wall with a painting and instead a bipartite decorative scheme was chosen, a solution frequently adopted in the case of small rooms. In addition, it was decided to let the white background of the wall, which illuminated the cubicle, emerge through the light structures, mostly painted in golden yellow, illuminated only by the open door in the wall E on the small peristyle. The abundance of the plant element, present everywhere in the small room (in the central compartment of the plinth, in the glimpses in the center of the middle area, in the long cane stalks), together with the variety of decorative elements, constitutes one of the elements of attraction of this pleasant and simple decoration which, according to M. de Vos (P Roma, p. 129, note 27), would represent "the highest level reached" by the Painters' Workshop in Via di Castricio. IV style.
